title_en: A Media & Culture Co., Ltd. v. National Intellectual Property Administration, et al. — administrative dispute over trademark opposition re-examination
ruling_gist_en: China's Trademark Law adopts a system where trademark rights are acquired through registration and follows the first-to-file principle. It does not require that only prior-use trademarks may apply for registration, nor does it stipulate that co-use of a trademark or co-contribution to trademark goodwill results in joint ownership of the trademark right. In the absence of clear legal provisions and a contractual basis, one cannot apply the concept of common property to conclude that trademark goodwill should be shared, thereby denying the applicant's legitimate qualification for prior trademark registration.
keywords_en: Administration; Administrative dispute over trademark opposition review; Retrial; Supreme People's Court; Beijing Municipality; Hainan Province; Legal person; State organ; Trademark Law; First-to-file principle for trademark registration; Whether co-use of trademark creates co-ownership rights; Registering by improper means a trademark that has been used by others and has certain influence; Reversal of judgment; Trademark opposition review; Right to the name of a TV program; Co-production of TV programs; Clarifying the application of the first-to-file principle for trademark registration; Rejecting the view that co-use of trademark creates co-ownership rights; Trademark right; Application for retrial; Trademark registration; Intellectual property; Administrative dispute over trademark opposition review (Bureau, etc.)
full_text_en:
【Ruling Gist】

China's Trademark Law adopts the system of trademark right acquisition through registration and the principle of first-to-file. It does not stipulate that only prior users of a mark may apply for registration, nor does it provide that co-users of a mark or those who have jointly contributed to the mark's goodwill become co-owners of the trademark right. In the absence of explicit statutory provisions and contractual basis, the approach of treating property as co-owned cannot be adopted to conclude that the goodwill embodied in a mark should be shared, nor can the legitimate qualification of an applicant who first files for trademark registration be denied.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2021) Zui Gao Fa Xing Zai No. 261

Re-applicant (plaintiff at first instance, appellee at second instance): A Media & Culture Co., Ltd. Domicile: Mentougou District, Beijing.

Legal representative: Li Moujia, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Li Jianfang, attorney at Beijing Zhongzhi Law Firm.

Respondent (third party at first instance, appellant at second instance): A Satellite TV Media Co., Ltd. Domicile: Haikou City, Hainan Province.

Legal representative: Gu Mou, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhu Xiaoyu, attorney at Beijing Jiaguan Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Li Ping, attorney at Beijing Jiaguan Law Firm.

Defendant at first instance: National Intellectual Property Administration. Domicile: Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal representative: Shen Mou, Director General.

Agent ad litem: Jia Mou, Examiner of the Administration.

The re-applicant A Media & Culture Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as A Media Company), in a dispute with the respondent A Satellite TV Media Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as A Satellite TV Company) and the defendant at first instance, the National Intellectual Property Administration, over an administrative case concerning trademark opposition review, appealed against the administrative judgment (2018) Jing Xing Zhong No. 4403 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court, and applied to this Court for retrial. On June 25, 2021, this Court issued the administrative ruling (2019) Zui Gao Fa Xing Shen No. 7392, granting retrial of this case. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on November 25, 2021. Li Jianfang, agent ad litem of the re-applicant A Media Company, Zhu Xiaoyu and Li Ping, agents ad litem of A Satellite TV Company, and Jia Mou, agent ad litem of the defendant at first instance, the National Intellectual Property Administration, appeared before the court to participate in the proceedings. The trial of this case has now been concluded.

The Beijing Intellectual Property Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) found the following facts upon trial: The trademark "Beautiful Beauty and device" No. 6****83 (hereinafter referred to as the trademark in dispute) was filed for registration by A Media Company with the Trademark Office of the former State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Office) on August 29, 2008, designated for use in Class 41 services, including "school (education), training, organization of educational or entertainment competitions, organization of cultural or educational exhibitions, arrangement and organization of training courses, organization of beauty pageants, organization of performances (shows), organization of fashion exhibitions for entertainment performances, libraries for lending books, text publishing (other than advertising brochures), book publishing, book publishing houses, online electronic book and magazine publishing, provision of online electronic publications (non-downloadable), film production, radio and television program production, drama production, performance production, program production, television entertainment programs, entertainment activities, performances, club services (entertainment or education), entertainment information, entertainment information (recreation), and fitness club services." It was preliminarily approved and published by the Trademark Office on November 6, 2012.

The trademark "Beautiful Beauty" No. 3****49 (hereinafter referred to as the cited trademark) was filed for registration by a third party, Guangzhou A Cultural Communication Co., Ltd., with the Trademark Office on August 1, 2002, and was approved for registration on March 21, 2004. The term of trademark exclusive right, after renewal, extends to March 20, 2024. It is approved for use in Class 41 services, including "radio and television program production."

A Satellite TV Company filed an opposition against the trademark in dispute within the statutory opposition period. On March 12, 2014, the Trademark Office issued the "Opposition Ruling on the trademark 'Beautiful Beauty'" [(2014) Trademark Opposition No. 337], determining that the trademark in dispute and the cited trademark did not constitute similar marks used on similar services, and did not violate the provisions of Articles 10 and 31 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2001) (hereinafter referred to as the 2001 Trademark Law), and thus approved the registration of the trademark in dispute.

A Satellite TV Company, dissatisfied with the ruling, filed an application for opposition review with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the former State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review Board) on April 10, 2014. On July 7, 2015, the Trademark Review Board issued the "Review Ruling on Opposition to the trademark 'Beautiful Beauty and device' No. 6****83" [Shang Ping Zi (2015) No. 47798] (hereinafter referred to as Ruling No. 47798), which held as follows:

Regarding whether the trademark in dispute and the cited trademark constituted "similar marks used on the same or similar goods" under Article 30 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (revised in 2013) (hereinafter referred to as the 2013 Trademark Law): Considering that the trademark in dispute had already attained a relatively high degree of recognition among the relevant public in services such as "program production" and "television entertainment programs," and that there were certain differences in the textual composition, pronunciation, and meaning between the trademark in dispute and the cited trademark, the two marks did not constitute similar marks. Therefore, registration of the trademark in dispute would not likely cause confusion or misidentification among consumers as to the source of services, and it did not constitute "similar marks used on the same or similar services" under Article 30 of the 2013 Trademark Law.

Regarding the claim of A Satellite TV Company concerning the right to the column name "Beautiful Beauty": A television column name objectively serves to identify the source of specific services (radio and television program production services) and can be treated as a trademark sign. Therefore, this ground for review by A Satellite TV Company essentially pertains to the expression of prior trademark rights. Moreover, apart from the claim of prior trademark rights, A Satellite TV Company did not specify which of its prior rights had been infringed by the registration of the trademark in dispute, nor did it provide evidence in this regard. Therefore, the Trademark Review Board combined this ground with the claim of trademark rights made by A Satellite TV Company for further elaboration.

The Trademark Review Board found that the television program "Beautiful Beauty" was co-produced and broadcast by A Satellite TV Company and A Media Company. The parties had also restricted their respective rights, obligations, and allocation of relevant commercial interests through written agreements. Before the date of filing for registration of the trademark in dispute, the television program "Beautiful Beauty" had already attained a relatively high degree of recognition among the relevant public, having been awarded the "Annual Social Production TV Program with the Greatest Online Influence in China" for five consecutive years. Therefore, it should be found in this case that "Beautiful Beauty," as a trademark used in services such as television entertainment activities, had become well-known to the relevant public and had achieved a certain social reputation. The property value carried by the text "Beautiful Beauty" was realized jointly by A Satellite TV Company and A Media Company, and both parties were entitled to the goodwill carried behind "Beautiful Beauty" and to engage in continuous market operations. Thus, "Beautiful Beauty" should not be exclusively owned or monopolized by A Media Company alone. If the trademark in dispute were approved for registration, it would likely hinder the realization of A Satellite TV Company's lawful rights and interests. Considering the above facts, from the perspective of safeguarding the actual interests of both parties, the registration of the trademark in dispute for the eighteen items of services, including "radio and television program production," violated the provision of Article 32 of the 2013 Trademark Law that "application for trademark registration shall not, by improper means, preemptively register a mark that has been used by another person and has acquired certain influence," and thus should not be approved for registration. The trademark in dispute was approved for registration for the remaining services.

The trademark in dispute did not have a negative or adverse impact on social public interests or public order, and did not violate the provisions of Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item 8 of the 2013 Trademark Law. Article 9 of the 2013 Trademark Law is a general provision. Since the Trademark Review Board had already applied the substantive provisions of the 2013 Trademark Law in its examination of this case, no further elaboration was necessary.

In summary, the Trademark Review Board ruled as follows: The trademark in dispute was not approved for registration in respect of "organization of educational or entertainment competitions, organization of cultural or educational exhibitions, arrangement and organization of training courses, organization of beauty pageants, organization of performances (shows), organization of fashion exhibitions for entertainment performances, film production, radio and television program production, drama production, performance production, program production, television entertainment programs, entertainment activities, performances, club services (entertainment or education), entertainment information, entertainment information (recreation), and fitness club services"; it was approved for registration in respect of the remaining services.

A Media Company, dissatisfied with Ruling No. 47798, filed an action with the court of first instance. Its main contentions were as follows: "Beautiful Beauty" was a trademark first used by A Media Company and had acquired a certain influence. Through continuous promotion and use of the trademark, A Media Company had made it well-known to the relevant public, thereby achieving a certain social reputation and influence. A Media Company's application for registration of the trademark in dispute was lawful and reasonable, without any bad faith, and would not hinder the realization of A Satellite TV Company's lawful rights and interests. It did not constitute a preemptive registration of another person's mark that had been used and had acquired a certain influence by improper means. Ruling No. 47798 was based on unclear facts and erroneous application of law. It requested the court to annul the ruling in accordance with the law and order the Trademark Review Board to make a new ruling.

The court of first instance found the following facts upon trial: A Media Company was established on April 16, 2003, with a registered capital of RMB 10 million. Its business scope included production and distribution of cartoons, television variety shows, feature films, etc.

On September 25, 2005, Beijing A Culture and Arts Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing A Culture Company) entered into an agreement with the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts, stipulating that Beijing A Culture Company would rent the theater studio of the Academy to record the program "Beautiful Beauty." Beijing A Culture Company paid the corresponding studio rental fee of RMB 35,000 to the Academy. On November 9, 2005, Li Mouyi, the host of the program "Beautiful Beauty," recorded in a blog post titled "A Bit Awkward Today": "I am recording a program called 'Beautiful Beauty.' The program has been in preparation for less than a month." On November 27, 2010, Li Mouyi recorded in a blog post titled "Beautiful Beauty's 5th Birthday": "Suddenly, 'Beautiful Beauty' has turned five. Our first recording was exactly on October 27, five years ago." From July to October 2005, Xu Mou was entrusted by Beijing A Culture Company to participate in the design of the program name and stage design for "Beautiful Beauty," and participated in the first recording of the program "Beautiful Beauty" in the theater studio of the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts in October 2005.

From January 2006, A Media Company (along with Beijing A Culture Company) entered into multiple cooperation agreements with A Satellite TV Company. In these cooperation agreements, the parties stipulated that A Media Company would produce each episode of the column "Beautiful Beauty" and would exclusively broadcast it through "A Satellite TV," with the copyright of each episode shared by both parties. The cooperation agreements also stipulated the respective rights, obligations, and allocation of relevant commercial interests. On January 21, 2006, the program "Beautiful Beauty" was first broadcast on A Satellite TV Company. The cooperation between A Media Company and A Satellite TV Company regarding the program "Beautiful Beauty" lasted from January 2006 until December 31, 2012.

On January 15, 2008, Beijing A Culture Company and A Media Company entered into a copyright assignment contract. The assignor was Beijing A Culture Company, and the assignee was A Media Company. The contract stipulated that the assignor, Beijing A Culture Company, and the relevant cooperating television stations jointly owned the copyright of the television programs listed in Appendix 2 to the contract. The assignor agreed to assign the rights in the television programs listed in Appendix 2 to the assignee, and the assignee agreed to accept such assignment. The assignor would make its best efforts to obtain the consent of the relevant cooperating television stations to such assignment. If the assignor could not obtain such consent, rendering the assignment impossible, the parties agreed that the assignor should assist the assignee to obtain any and all rights and interests that the assignee would be entitled to as a co-owner of the copyright of the television programs listed in Appendix 2. Appendix 2 to the contract indicated that the cooperating television station for "Beautiful Beauty" was A Satellite TV, with a cooperation period from 2006 to 2007, totaling 312 episodes.

On April 21, 2011, Beijing A Culture Company was cancelled by the Fengtai Branch of Beijing Administration for Industry and Commerce.

A Media Company submitted a copyright registration certificate for the artistic work "Beautiful Beauty," with a registration date of June 26, 2012, which A Media Company enjoyed as a legal entity copyright owner.

On November 16, 2015, Ma Mou and Li Moujia, as declarants, issued a "Statement on Copyright Assignment," stating: Before the cancellation of Beijing A Culture Company, the declarants (Ma Mou and Li Moujia) were shareholders of Beijing A Culture Company, each having contributed RMB 100,000 in cash. After the company's cancellation, the declarants discovered that the copyright of the artistic work "Beautiful Beauty," owned by Beijing A Culture Company, had not been explicitly disposed of during the liquidation. The declarants hereby clarify that, effective from January 15, 2008, all rights and interests owned by Beijing A Culture Company, including the copyright of the artistic work "Beautiful Beauty," were transferred to A Media Company. A Media Company has the right to handle all legal matters related to the aforementioned rights and interests.

The court of first instance held: This case should be examined under the 2013 Trademark Law. Regarding whether the trademark in dispute constituted a "mark that has been used by another person and has acquired a certain influence, which was preemptively registered by improper means" under Article 32 of the 2013 Trademark Law, the facts found in this case were as follows:

First, according to the copyright assignment contract between Beijing A Culture Company and A Media Company, Beijing A Culture Company assigned to A Media Company the copyright it owned in the program "Beautiful Beauty." Subsequently, A Media Company entered into multiple cooperation agreements with A Satellite TV Company regarding the production and broadcast of the program "Beautiful Beauty." Therefore, A Media Company had actually succeeded to the copyright and related rights and interests in the program "Beautiful Beauty" originally owned by Beijing A Culture Company.

Second, the agreement and invoices for renting the studio to record the column "Beautiful Beauty" entered into between Beijing A Culture Company and the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts on September 25, 2005; the blog posts published by Li Mouyi, the founder of the program "Beautiful Beauty," on Sina Blog, including "Beautiful Beauty's 5th Birthday" and "A Bit Awkward Today," authenticated by the Notarial Certificate (2015) Jing Fangyuan Nei Jing Zheng Zi No. 28631; the video screenshots of the program "Beautiful Beauty" showing the stage designer as Xu Mou, together with Xu Mou's identity documents and testimony; and other evidence proved that the television program "Beautiful Beauty" was prepared and first produced by Beijing A Culture Company starting from the second half of 2005, and that the brand concept and design of the program originated from Beijing A Culture Company.

Third, according to the contents of multiple cooperation agreements between A Media Company and A Satellite TV Company, the parties explicitly stipulated that the program "Beautiful Beauty" was produced by A Media Company and exclusively broadcast through "A Satellite TV," and they also explicitly stipulated their respective rights, obligations, and allocation of relevant commercial interests. On January 21, 2006, the program "Beautiful Beauty" was first broadcast on A Satellite TV, and thereafter continued to be broadcast on that platform until December 31, 2012. According to awards received by the program "Beautiful Beauty," it had been awarded the "Annual Social Production TV Program with the Greatest Online Influence in China" for five consecutive years. Prior to the date of filing for registration of the trademark in dispute, August 29, 2008, the television program "Beautiful Beauty" had already attained a relatively high degree of recognition among the relevant public. "Beautiful Beauty," as the specific program name of the television program "Beautiful Beauty," actually served to distinguish the source of television program services during the production and broadcast of the program, and could be recognized as trademark use. Therefore, "Beautiful Beauty," as a trademark continuously used in services such as television entertainment activities, had become well-known to the relevant public and constituted a mark that had been used prior to registration and had acquired a certain influence.

Fourth, reviewing all evidence in this case, before the date of filing for registration of the trademark in dispute, A Media Company and A Satellite TV Company had no special agreement on the attribution of the sign "Beautiful Beauty."

Considering the above facts comprehensively, the court of first instance held that China's Trademark Law adopts the principle of first-to-file for trademark registration. Unlike the Patent Law or the Copyright Law, the Trademark Law does not contain provisions similar to "the person who creates the work is the author" or "the person who makes a substantive contribution to the technical solution of the invention is the inventor." Therefore, in the absence of other legal or contractual basis, the conclusion that "co-users of a mark are co-owners of trademark rights" cannot be drawn by analogy. In this case, A Media Company (Beijing A Culture Company) began preparing and first producing the program "Beautiful Beauty" in the second half of 2005, and the brand concept and design of the program originated from A Media Company. The cooperation agreements between A Media Company and A Satellite TV Company also explicitly stipulated that the program "Beautiful Beauty" was produced by A Media Company and exclusively broadcast through "A Satellite TV." Subsequently, the program "Beautiful Beauty" was first broadcast on A Satellite TV on January 21, 2006, which was obviously later than the time A Media Company prepared and produced the program. Therefore, A Satellite TV Company did not have the fact of prior use of the sign "Beautiful Beauty." Although it cannot be denied that the program "Beautiful Beauty" became well-known to the relevant public due to continuous broadcast through "A Satellite TV" and thereby gained a certain social reputation, this does not mean that A Satellite TV Company automatically acquired a "co-ownership of trademark right" in the sign "Beautiful Beauty." Given that A Media Company applied for registration of the trademark in dispute first, and its use of the sign "Beautiful Beauty" also preceded that of A Satellite TV Company, there was no fact of A Media Company preemptively registering a mark that had been used by A Satellite TV Company and had acquired a certain influence. Naturally, there was no subjective bad faith on the part of A Media Company to preemptively register the goodwill attached to a mark used by A Satellite TV Company and having a certain influence. Therefore, A Media Company's application for registration of the trademark in dispute complied with legal provisions and did not violate the principle of good faith. The application for registration of the trademark in dispute in respect of services such as "radio and television program production" did not constitute the circumstance described in Article 32 of the 2013 Trademark Law of "preemptively registering, by improper means, a mark that has been used by another person and has acquired a certain influence." The relevant findings in Ruling No. 47798 were erroneous, and the court of first instance corrected them in accordance with the law.

In summary, the court of first instance, in accordance with Items (1) and (2) of Article 70 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment: Ruling No. 47798 was annulled; the Trademark Review Board was to make a new ruling. The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 was to be borne by the Trademark Review Board.

A satellite TV company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance), requesting the revocation of the first-instance judgment and the maintenance of Ruling No. 47798. The main reasons were: (1) As a co-owner of the copyright in the program "Beautiful Beauties," the satellite TV company argued that, absent its consent to the relevant assignment by a Beijing culture company, it could not be determined that a media company had actually succeeded to the copyright and related rights and interests that the Beijing culture company enjoyed in the "Beautiful Beauties" program. (2) The media company and the Beijing culture company are not the same entity and should not be conflated. The media company began participating in the production of the "Beautiful Beauties" program in January 2008, and it did not use the program name and the "Beautiful Beauties" mark earlier than the satellite TV company. (3) Prior to the filing date of the trademark in dispute, the influence of the "Beautiful Beauties" program was jointly created by the satellite TV company and the Beijing culture company, and the goodwill it carried should also be jointly enjoyed by the satellite TV company and the Beijing culture company, and was unrelated to the media company. The "Beautiful Beauties" program, through long-term use by the satellite TV company, had established a unique association with the satellite TV company. The media company, knowing this, still applied to register "Beautiful Beauties," harming the satellite TV company's prior rights in the program name, and constituting an act of preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark that others had already used and had a certain influence. In 2012, after the media company terminated its cooperation with the satellite TV company, it cooperated with Heilongjiang Satellite TV and Anhui Satellite TV to produce and broadcast a television program of the same name. The existence of two television programs with the same name broadcast on different satellite television channels would cause confusion and misidentification among the relevant public. (4) The media company, as a partner of the satellite TV company, knowing of the existence of the trademark in dispute, preemptively registered it, which constituted malicious preemptive registration under Article 15 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment). In summary, the trademark in dispute should not be approved for registration.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and the media company did not appeal the first-instance judgment.

The court of second instance affirmed the facts found by the court of first instance.

The court of second instance held that, under Article 32 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment), it was necessary to determine whether the trademark for which protection was claimed was a trademark that had been used prior, and whether that trademark had a certain influence. In this case, although the media company submitted a "Copyright Assignment Contract" signed with the Beijing culture company, that contract was an agreement between the parties on the ownership of copyright and did not stipulate the rights to the relevant trademark mark. Moreover, the media company and the Beijing culture company are different legal entities and cannot be conflated. Therefore, the use of "Beautiful Beauties" by the Beijing culture company cannot be equated with use by the media company. The court of first instance conflated the two, and the court of second instance hereby corrects that.

The media company submitted evidence including a venue lease agreement signed between the Beijing culture company and the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts in September 2005, an advertising cooperation agreement signed by the Beijing culture company in December 2005, microblogs of the host of the "Beautiful Beauties" program, and witness testimony, in an attempt to prove that it had used the "Beautiful Beauties" trademark prior to others. First, as stated above, the use by the Beijing culture company cannot be conflated with the use by the media company. Second, the above-mentioned use by the Beijing culture company does not constitute "trademark use" within the meaning of the Trademark Law. The services designated by the trademark in dispute include "broadcasting and television program production" and the like. Only when the mark is used in connection with the above services, and through such use the relevant public can recognize it as a trademark, thereby distinguishing the source of goods and services, does such use constitute trademark use and give rise to rights in an unregistered trademark. If a program name is to give rise to rights in an unregistered trademark in services such as "broadcasting and television program production," it is necessary to consider the specific manner of use of the mark; that is, it must be used on the above services to become an unregistered trademark. For unregistered marks used on services such as "broadcasting and television program production," the focus should be on the provision of production services, and the name of the produced program should not be conflated with the production services provided; for marks used on services such as "television entertainment programs, entertainment activities, performances, club services (entertainment or education), entertainment information, entertainment information (recreation)," such marks should be attached to programs or information, and for programs or information that are still in the process of production and not yet completed, no rights in an unregistered trademark can arise. Regarding the other reviewed services of the trademark in dispute, the media company did not submit evidence of prior use earlier than that of the satellite TV company. In summary, the evidence submitted by the media company, including the venue lease agreement, advertising cooperation agreement, and the host's microblogs, can only prove that the Beijing culture company used "Beautiful Beauties" as a program name in the process of creating the work, but cannot prove that the Beijing culture company used "Beautiful Beauties" as a trademark prior to others.

The trademark in dispute was filed for registration on August 29, 2008. Prior to that date, the "Beautiful Beauties" program had been broadcast on the satellite TV company's platform since January 2006. The satellite TV company and the Beijing culture company entered into cooperation agreements in 2006 and 2007 respectively. The 2006 agreement stipulated that the Beijing culture company would provide program proposals to the satellite TV company, and after written review and confirmation by the satellite TV company, the Beijing culture company would plan and produce the program and broadcast it on the satellite TV company's channel; the Beijing culture company would submit the program produced according to the satellite TV company's requirements on time for broadcast. The 2007 agreement stipulated that the "Beautiful Beauties" program would be jointly invested by both parties and the Beijing culture company would be commissioned to produce it. In 2008, the satellite TV company entered into a cooperation agreement with the media company, stipulating that the "Beautiful Beauties" program would be jointly invested by both parties and the satellite TV company would commission the media company to produce it. The cooperation agreement between the satellite TV company and the media company lasted until 2012. Since its premiere on the satellite TV company's channel in 2006, the "Beautiful Beauties" program had received multiple honors. Before the filing date of the trademark in dispute, the "Beautiful Beauties" mark, as the name of the program, had been disseminated and used through the satellite TV company's platform, leading the relevant public to identify it as a television entertainment program, thereby having the function of distinguishing the source of goods or services and constituting an unregistered trademark within the meaning of the Trademark Law. Moreover, the satellite TV company's use had also made the "Beautiful Beauties" television program well known among the relevant public. Therefore, the satellite TV company's "Beautiful Beauties" mark, as a trademark used in services such as television entertainment activities, had become well known to the relevant public before the filing date of the trademark in dispute, and constituted a trademark that had been used prior and had a certain influence.

In summary, where the "Beautiful Beauties" mark, as a trademark used in services such as television entertainment activities, had become well known to the relevant public through use and promotion by the satellite TV company, and constituted a "trademark that had been used prior and had a certain influence," the media company, knowing of the existence of the mark, applied to register it as the trademark in dispute in this case. Its conduct constituted the circumstance of "preemptively registering, by improper means, a trademark that another person has already used and has a certain influence" as stipulated in Article 32 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment). Therefore, the relevant grounds of appeal of the satellite TV company were established, and the court of second instance upheld them.

In this case, the satellite TV company also claimed that the application for registration of the trademark in dispute infringed its "right to program name." According to the relevant provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China, if a program name has a certain degree of popularity, it can be protected as a "product name with certain influence." However, a "product name with certain influence" is essentially still an unregistered trademark, and the standard for protection also depends on whether it causes confusion as to the source of the product. Therefore, when the satellite TV company simultaneously claims a "trademark that has been used prior and has a certain influence," further protection under "right to program name" is unnecessary. Hence, the relevant grounds of appeal of the satellite TV company could not be established, and the court of second instance did not support them.

In the opposition application grounds submitted by the satellite TV company during the trademark review stage, it did not raise the issue of whether the trademark in dispute violated Article 15 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment). Therefore, whether the trademark in dispute violated Article 15 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment) was not within the scope of trial of this case, and the court of second instance did not comment on it.

This case is an administrative dispute over trademark authorization and confirmation. The satellite TV company's claims regarding copyright issues related to the "Beautiful Beauties" program are not within the scope of trial of this case. Therefore, the relevant grounds of appeal of the satellite TV company could not be established, and the court of second instance did not support them.

In summary, in accordance with Article 69 and Article 89, Paragraph 1, Item 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of second instance rendered the following judgment: revoke the first-instance judgment and reject the claims of the media company. The case acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 100, shall be borne by the media company.

The media company applied for retrial, claiming: (1) Both the Beijing culture company and the media company had engaged in trademark use of the "Beautiful Beauties" mark in connection with "program production" services in Class 41 of the Classification of Similar Goods and Services, and had no bad faith in applying for the trademark in dispute. The use of the trademark in dispute by the Beijing culture company and the media company in program names, office premises, etc., constituted typical use within Class 41 services. Program production is independent of broadcasting platforms and exists independently; broadcasting is not a prerequisite for production services. At the same time, the media company had carried out a series of actions to protect civil rights against others damaging the relevant civil rights related to the "Beautiful Beauties" mark. (2) The media company used the trademark in dispute prior to others, so there was no basis for applying the provision "preemptively registering, by improper means, a trademark that another person has already used and has a certain influence." The Beijing culture company had completed production of the "Beautiful Beauties" program and used the trademark in dispute before it contacted the satellite TV company. After the broadcast of the "Beautiful Beauties" program, it was still the Beijing culture company and the media company that directly used the trademark in dispute in connection with Class 41 services, not the satellite TV company. The satellite TV company's act of broadcasting the "Beautiful Beauties" program fell under Class 38 "television broadcasting" services. Viewers can also distinguish between the producer and broadcaster of a television program. For programs that have gained high popularity through broadcasting, the program name and corresponding trademark rights in Class 41 services do not transfer to the television station. The cooperation agreements signed by both parties clearly stated that the media company and the Beijing culture company were the producers of the program, and the satellite TV company did not participate in production and could not be the user of Class 41 services. The satellite TV company was not an interested party in this case and had no right to file an opposition or request for opposition review. (3) The media company's application for registration of the trademark in dispute was in line with the interests of the media company, the Beijing culture company, and their shareholders, and did not harm the interests of others. The media company and the Beijing culture company were both founded by host Li B (Li Yi), have the same business, and their main staff overlap; the legal representative of the Beijing culture company is Yu (Yu), and the supervisor is Li A (Li Jia); the supervisor of the media company is Yu (Yu), and the legal representative is Li A (Li Jia). The two companies have unity of expression of intent and consistency of business interests. (4) Under the policy of "separation of production and broadcasting," program production is independent of broadcasting platforms and exists completely independently. The program name naturally belongs to the production company, serving to identify the source of services. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, the program name and corresponding trademark rights should belong to the producer, who has the right to protect the programs it produces. As a broadcasting platform, all intellectual property rights enjoyed by the satellite TV company in relation to the program derived from contracts, and it had no right to claim or exercise rights beyond the contracts. In summary, the media company requested this Court to revoke the second-instance judgment and, by amendment, uphold the first-instance judgment.

The satellite TV company argued in defense: (1) The media company and the Beijing culture company are different legal entities and cannot be conflated; the Beijing culture company's use of the program name "Beautiful Beauties" cannot be deemed use by the media company. The satellite TV company and the Beijing culture company were the first to cooperate in producing and broadcasting the "Beautiful Beauties" program and using the trademark in dispute, and agreed on joint ownership of copyright. The media company only began participating in production in January 2008, and its use of the program name and the trademark in dispute was later than that of the satellite TV company. The satellite TV company is a co-owner of the copyright and related rights in the "Beautiful Beauties" program. Without the consent of the satellite TV company to the relevant assignment, the media company's acquisition of the copyright in the "Beautiful Beauties" program is invalid, and the media company did not actually succeed to the copyright and related rights enjoyed by the Beijing culture company in the "Beautiful Beauties" program. The satellite TV company's commissioning of the media company to continue producing subsequent episodes should not be deemed as the satellite TV company's recognition of the assignment between the Beijing culture company and the media company. (2) The Beijing culture company did not use "Beautiful Beauties" as a trademark. All preparatory work by the Beijing culture company before January 2006 was done to fulfill its cooperation agreement with the satellite TV company, and "Beautiful Beauties" was used solely as a program name. The media company did not submit evidence that the Beijing culture company used the program name "Beautiful Beauties" in office premises, program recording venues, etc., earlier than the satellite TV company, nor did it provide evidence that the Beijing culture company had completed production and publicly released the program before cooperating with the satellite TV company. (3) Through two years of use by the satellite TV company, the program name "Beautiful Beauties" had acquired the function of identifying the source of specific services, constituting a trademark that had been used prior and had a certain influence. Since its premiere in 2006, the "Beautiful Beauties" program has prominently displayed the satellite TV company's logo in the upper left corner of each episode's screen, and the program name appears repeatedly in the opening, middle, and closing credits. The closing credits of each episode list "Satellite TV Company, Beijing Mou Culture and Art Development Co., Ltd." The program name and stage design are components of the program, and the related rights are jointly owned by the satellite TV company and the Beijing culture company. (4) Without the consent of the satellite TV company, the media company unilaterally applied for and intended to exclusively own the trademark in dispute, violating the latter part of Article 32 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment). It requested this Court to reject the media company's application for retrial.

The National Intellectual Property Administration stated that the second-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. It requested that the second-instance judgment and Ruling No. 47798 be upheld.

During the retrial review stage, the media company submitted the following evidence to this Court:

Evidence 1-3: Partial recording notices for the "Beautiful Beauties" program; partial scripts, materials, dubbing, etc. of the "Beautiful Beauties" program recorded by the media company; partial broadcast schedules and annual broadcast summaries of the "Beautiful Beauties" program produced by the media company. Used to prove that the Beijing culture company and the media company were engaged in Class 41 program production services, while the satellite TV company, which provided the broadcast platform, was not actually engaged in Class 41 program production services, and its broadcast conduct fell under Class 38 television broadcasting.

Evidence 4: Images showing the use of the "Beautiful Beauties" mark in office premises, recording sites, etc. Used to prove that the use of the trademark in dispute by the Beijing culture company and the media company constituted trademark use.

Evidence 5: Full video and partial screenshots of the first episode of "Beautiful Beauties" titled "Versatile Black." Used to prove that the Beijing culture company and the media company used the "Beautiful Beauties" trademark prior in connection with Class 41 program production services.

Evidence 6: Relationship chart between the media company and the Beijing culture company. Used to prove that the use of the "Beautiful Beauties" mark by the media company and the Beijing culture company should be considered as a whole.

Evidence 7: Policies and discussions on the separation of production and broadcasting. Used to prove that, under the policy background of separation of production and broadcasting, the media company and the satellite TV company provide different services, namely "program production" and "program (television) broadcasting."

Evidence 8: Civil judgment (2017) Hu 73 Min Zhong No. 282 of the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court. Used to prove that the media company, as the rights holder of the "Beautiful Beauties" program name, had actually carried out rights enforcement actions.

Evidence 9-10: Venue lease cooperation agreement signed between the Beijing culture company and the Audio-Visual Education Center of Beijing University of Technology on December 26, 2006; original records of discussions on the production details of specific themed episodes of "Beautiful Beauties" on December 17, 2006. Used to prove that the Beijing culture company was the true provider of program production services.

Evidence 11-13: Agreement on the general transfer of fixed assets from the Beijing culture company to the media company in 2008; domain name transfer agreement changing the domain name of the Beijing culture company to the media company in 2008; trademark assignment contract for the transfer of related trademarks from the Beijing culture company to the media company in 2008. Used to prove that the media company had the right to apply for registration of the trademark in dispute.

Evidence 14: Marriage certificate of the legal representative of the Beijing culture company, Yu, and the legal representative of the media company, Li A (Li Jia). Used to prove the relationship between the Beijing culture company and the media company.

Evidence 15-17: List of credited cast and crew at the end of "Beautiful Beauties" episodes; list and labor contracts of current employees involved in the production of "Beautiful Beauties"; list and labor contracts of former employees involved in the production of "Beautiful Beauties." Used to prove that the media company had been continuously engaged in the production of the "Beautiful Beauties" program.

Evidence 18: Books related to broadcasting and television. Used to prove that program production and broadcasting are independent and entirely different tasks.

Evidence 19: Photos of the "Beautiful Beauties" production team participating in earthquake relief. Used to prove that the media company participated in earthquake relief in the name of the "Beautiful Beauties" production team.

The satellite TV company expressed the following opinions on the above evidence: it did not recognize the authenticity, relevance, or probative purpose of Evidence 1-4, 8-13, and 19; it recognized the authenticity of Evidence 5-7 and 14-18, but not their relevance or probative purpose. The National Intellectual Property Administration recognized the authenticity of the above evidence, but not its relevance.

This Court confirms the authenticity of Evidence 5-8 and 14-18; their relevance and other aspects will be discussed in conjunction with the original trial evidence and the issues in dispute in the opinion section of this Court.

This Court finds upon retrial that the facts found in the first-instance and second-instance judgments are clear, and this Court affirms them.

It is further found that, in accordance with the institutional reform deployment of the central authorities, the relevant functions and responsibilities of the Trademark Office and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board are now uniformly exercised by the National Intellectual Property Administration.

This Court considers that the issue in dispute in the retrial stage of this case is: whether the application for registration of the trademark in dispute violates the latter part of Article 32 of the Trademark Law (2013 Amendment) which provides that "no trademark may be registered by preemptive registration by improper means of a trademark that another person has already used and has a certain influence."

Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013 provides: "No trademark application for registration may infringe upon another person's existing prior rights, nor may it, by unfair means, preemptively register a trademark that another person has already used and has a certain influence." Article 23 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation provides: "Where a prior user claims that a trademark applicant has, by unfair means, preemptively registered a trademark that it has used and has a certain influence, if the prior used trademark has a certain influence and the trademark applicant knew or should have known of the trademark, it may be presumed that the applicant has 'preemptively registered by unfair means.' However, this does not apply if the trademark applicant provides evidence proving that it had no malicious intent to exploit the goodwill of the prior used trademark. If the prior user provides evidence showing that its prior trademark has been used continuously for a certain period, within a certain region, or with a certain sales volume or advertising, the people's court may find that the trademark has a certain influence. If the prior user claims that the trademark applicant, by applying for registration of the prior used trademark that has a certain influence on goods that are not similar to its goods, violates the provisions of Article 32 of the Trademark Law, the people's court shall not support such claim." According to the above provisions, one of the constituent elements of the second half of Article 32 is that the trademark applicant has subjective malice, i.e., preemptively registering a trademark by unfair means.

In this case, the issue is whether Media Company A had subjective malice when applying for registration of the disputed trademark. The first instance found that the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program was prepared and produced by Beijing Cultural Company A starting in the second half of 2005. In 2006 and 2007, Beijing Cultural Company A and Satellite TV Company A entered into cooperation agreements, stipulating that the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program would be jointly invested in by both parties, produced by Beijing Cultural Company A, and the copyright in the program would be jointly owned by both parties. In January 2008, Media Company A and Satellite TV Company A entered into a cooperation agreement, stipulating that the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program would be jointly invested in by both parties, produced by Media Company A, and the copyright in the program would be jointly owned by both parties. In January 2006, the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program premiered on Satellite TV Company A's channel and was continuously broadcast on that platform until December 31, 2012. In January 2008, Beijing Cultural Company A and Media Company A entered into a contract, stipulating that Beijing Cultural Company A would transfer to Media Company A the copyright in the 2006 and 2007 "Meili Qiaojia Ren" TV program (a total of 312 episodes), which it jointly owned with Satellite TV Company A. After Beijing Cultural Company A was dissolved, its shareholders issued a statement clarifying that, effective January 15, 2008, all rights and interests, including the copyright in the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" artistic work, were transferred to Media Company A. Based on the above facts, the following analysis can be made: First, although the cooperation agreements successively entered into by Satellite TV Company A with Beijing Cultural Company A or Media Company A all stipulated that the parties jointly owned the copyright in the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program, they did not specify the ownership of rights and interests in "Meili Qiaojia Ren" as a trademark. Second, the disputed trademark in this case is a combined graphic and word mark, and the mark is identical to the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" artistic work. The "Meili Qiaojia Ren" artistic work was created in 2005 by Xu upon the commission of Beijing Cultural Company A, and the copyright belonged to Beijing Cultural Company A. After Beijing Cultural Company A was dissolved, the copyright in the artistic work was transferred to Media Company A. Third, the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program was initially planned and produced by Beijing Cultural Company A. Prior to the filing date of the disputed trademark, Media Company A had already actually engaged in producing the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program. Taking the above factors into comprehensive consideration, Media Company A filed an application for registration of the disputed trademark with the Trademark Office on August 29, 2008, for services in Class 41, such as "radio and television program production, television entertainment programs," which was legitimate and not subjectively malicious. Therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark did not violate the provision in the second half of Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013 that a trademark application for registration "may not, by unfair means, preemptively register a trademark that another person has already used and has a certain influence." The court of second instance failed to fully consider the applicable requirements of the second half of Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013, and its application of law was erroneous.

Regarding the issue raised in Ruling No. 47798 that both Satellite TV Company A and Media Company A share the goodwill embodied in the disputed trademark and that it should not be enjoyed exclusively by Media Company A: First, the second half of Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013 should be understood within the system of the Trademark Law. China's Trademark Law adopts a system of trademark rights acquired through registration. Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Trademark Law of 2013 provides: "Trademarks approved and registered by the Trademark Office are registered trademarks, including commodity trademarks, service marks, collective marks, and certification marks; the trademark registrant shall enjoy the exclusive right to use the trademark, which shall be protected by law." Article 4 provides: "Any natural person, legal person, or other organization that needs to acquire the exclusive right to use a trademark for its goods or services in the course of production or business operations shall file an application for trademark registration with the Trademark Office. The provisions of this Law concerning commodity trademarks shall apply to service marks." According to these provisions, the exclusive right to use a trademark is protected by law, and the way for relevant entities to acquire the exclusive right to use a trademark is to apply for trademark registration. However, in order to balance the interests of all parties and take into account the principle of fairness, China's Trademark Law also provides a certain degree of protection for unregistered trademarks, such as Article 13, paragraph 2, Article 15, the second half of Article 32, and Article 59, paragraph 3, of the Trademark Law of 2013. For unregistered trademarks that have been used first and have a certain influence, on the one hand, the second half of Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013 prohibits others from maliciously preemptively registering them; on the other hand, Article 59, paragraph 3, of the Trademark Law of 2013 allows the prior user to continue using the trademark within the original scope. Second, with respect to the ownership of rights, China's Trademark Law differs from the Copyright Law and the Patent Law. According to the Copyright Law, copyright generally belongs to the person who created the work, i.e., the author. For works created jointly by two or more persons, the copyright is jointly owned by the joint authors. According to the Patent Law, for non-service invention-creation, the right to apply for a patent belongs to the inventor or designer, i.e., the person who has made creative contributions to the substantive features of the invention-creation. For invention-creations completed through collaboration or commission, unless otherwise agreed, the right to apply for a patent belongs to the unit or individual that completed or jointly completed the invention-creation. In contrast, the Trademark Law adopts a first-to-file principle for trademark registration. According to Article 31 of the Trademark Law of 2013, preliminary approval and announcement are given to the trademark that is first filed; for trademarks filed on the same day, preliminary approval and announcement are given to the trademark that is first used. The Trademark Law neither stipulates that only a prior-used trademark may be applied for registration, nor does it provide that joint use of a trademark or joint contribution to the goodwill of a trademark results in joint ownership of the trademark right. Third, when an administrative authority determines whether a trademark applied for registration violates the second half of Article 32 of the Trademark Law of 2013, it must comprehensively analyze a series of constituent elements, such as whether the goodwill of the prior used trademark has reached a certain level of influence and whether the trademark applicant has the malicious intent to exploit the goodwill of the prior used trademark. As previously discussed, the applicant for the disputed trademark in this case, Media Company A, did not have the malicious intent to exploit the goodwill of another person's prior used trademark. Therefore, in the absence of explicit legal provisions and contractual basis, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board's analysis and judgment regarding goodwill contributions, and its adoption of a property co-ownership approach leading to the conclusion that Satellite TV Company A and Media Company A share the goodwill of the disputed trademark and precluding Media Company A's prior application, constituted an erroneous application of law.

Furthermore, with respect to the issue of whether Satellite TV Company A has the standing to file a trademark opposition and a request for review of the opposition. Article 6 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of Law in Trademark Cases after the Implementation of the Decision on Amending the Trademark Law provides that, for a request for review of a trademark opposition accepted before the implementation of the Decision on Amending the Trademark Law, where the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board, after the implementation of the Decision, makes a decision not to approve registration, and a party institutes administrative litigation, the people's court shall apply the pre-amendment Trademark Law when reviewing issues concerning the right of action and standing. According to the above provision, the Trademark Law of 2001 applies to the review of standing and the right of action in this case. Satellite TV Company A filed the trademark opposition and the request for review of the opposition under the Trademark Law of 2001. Article 30 of the Trademark Law of 2001 provides: "Any person may, within three months from the date of announcement of a trademark that has been preliminarily approved, file an opposition against it. If no opposition is filed upon expiration of the announcement period, the trademark shall be approved for registration, a trademark registration certificate shall be issued, and the trademark shall be announced." Article 33, paragraph 1, provides: "Where an opposition is filed against a trademark that has been preliminarily approved and announced, the Trademark Office shall hear the facts and reasons stated by the opposer and the opposed, and after investigation and verification, shall make a ruling. If a party is dissatisfied, it may, within fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice, apply to the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board for a review, and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board shall make a ruling and notify the opposer and the opposed in writing." Accordingly, the Trademark Law of 2001 imposes no restriction on the standing of a trademark opposer. At the same time, the facts ascertained in this case show that Satellite TV Company A was the broadcasting platform for the "Meili Qiaojia Ren" program and one of its copyright owners, and it has an interest in the registration of the disputed trademark. Media Company A's ground for retrial, that Satellite TV Company A is not an interested party in this case and is not entitled to file a trademark opposition or a request for review of the opposition, lacks factual and legal basis, and this court does not support it.

In summary, some of Media Company A's grounds for retrial are established. The judgment of the first instance is correct and should be affirmed. The judgment of the second instance contains an erroneous application of law and should be corrected. Pursuant to subparagraph (2) of paragraph 1 of Article 89 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and paragraph 1 of Article 119 and Article 122 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. Revoke Administrative Judgment No. (2018) Jing Xing Zhong 4403 of the Beijing High People's Court;

2. Affirm Administrative Judgment No. (2015) Jing Zhi Xing Chu 4913 of the Beijing Intellectual Property Court.

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne by the China National Intellectual Property Administration; the second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 100 shall be borne by Satellite TV Media Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
